title: The strange science of the yawn
text: A yawn {{1}} about six seconds, arrives unbidden, and is so universal that almost every vertebrate does it — yet science still cannot entirely explain it. No one is quite {{2}} why we yawn at all. The folk theory, that the body needs {{3}} oxygen, collapsed when experiments showed that breathing pure air changes nothing; the current favourite holds that yawning {{4}} the brain, like a fan in an overheated room, with the deep inhalation cooling blood on its way upstairs. Stranger still is the contagious kind. Contagious yawning {{5}} in children at around the age of four, the point at which the social emotions come online, and psychologists {{6}} it to empathy: people who yawn easily with others tend to score higher on tests of perspective-taking, and dogs, famously, catch yawns from their owners. Even {{7}} the womb, foetuses have been observed yawning mid-pregnancy. The yawn, in short, remains a matter of genuine scientific {{8}}: universal, ancient and oddly communicative, half-explained in an age of scanners — a reminder of how much remains unknown about the body we live in.

gaps.explanation: 'a yawn lasts about six seconds' — intransitive verb for duration.
'no one is quite sure why' — adjective after 'is'.
'yawning cools the brain' — the brain-cooling theory.
'contagious yawning kicks in at four' — phrasal verb: starts.
'attribute it to empathy' — attribute X to Y: assign the cause.
'even inside the womb' — stationary location, not movement.
'a matter of genuine scientific speculation' — open debate.
